abstract: Marine heatwaves exceeding species thermal optima impact survival outcomes that may be exacerbated by starvation. Here we tested whether food availability influences short-term heat stress effects on immune function, behaviour and metabolism with a leather star (Dermasterias imbricata). First, we experimentally tested immune response, growth, body condition and righting responses under two food treatments (access vs. restricted) and three temperatures (15, 20, or 25°C). In a second experiment, we measured respiration rate and resistance to a high temperature (28°C) in animals held at 10 or 15°C under the same food treatments. Overall, responses tracked expected temperature dependent rises. Yet long-term immersion at 25°C was detrimental under food restriction, leading to reduced immune responses, while righting success increased. We find that declining food availability during marine heatwaves could amplify thermal stress by forcing energetic trade-offs that compromise immune function and survival.
